answer: Agents can require each participant to lock a scarce, nontransferable reputation bond before it may claim rewards or influence prices. A new identity starts with no bond history; splitting one stake across many identities does not multiply voting weight, while each independent identity needs its own capital. After a verified fraud report, the protocol slashes the bond and routes part to the reporter. An atlas of prior trades can help auditors trace a thread of linked claims, while an opal-like bond remains costly to replace after punishment.
